query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for plasma-facing applications in fusion reactors, what single intervention could improve radiation tolerance while preserving mechanical integrity and engineering practicality? Formulate one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the proposed mechanism, predicts a measurable improvement over the unmodified baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites prior evidence supporting the causal rationale, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the titanium fraction (by partially replacing chromium) in a tungsten-based refractory HEA—for example, modifying the (CrFeTiTa)70W30 composition—will yield a more chemically homogeneous microstructure that impedes He bubble coarsening under irradiation, thereby enhancing radiation tolerance while maintaining mechanical integrity and manufacturability.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline is a refractory high‐entropy alloy such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30 produced via mechanical alloying and sintering (or additive manufacturing) that currently shows larger, coarser helium bubble formation under reactor‐relevant ion irradiation.
generation.intervention: Tailor the alloy composition by increasing the relative titanium content at the expense of chromium (or another element contributing to segregation) to achieve a more uniform microstructure.
generation.conditions: Testing should be performed under helium ion irradiation at reactor-relevant fluences and elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1023 K), with samples produced using additive manufacturing routes that emphasize compositional homogeneity.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform, single-phase BCC microstructure with reduced elemental segregation minimizes preferential sites for helium bubble nucleation and coarsening.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced titanium levels promote chemical complexity and microstructural homogeneity, which inhibits the coalescence and growth of helium bubbles. This stabilization reduces irradiation-induced hardening and possible embrittlement while preserving high-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The titanium-enhanced alloy will display significantly smaller and less dense helium bubbles and reduced irradiation-induced hardening (an expected improvement on the order of several percentage points relative to the baseline), with mechanical strength maintained at high temperatures comparable to or better than the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (CrFeTiTa)70W30 alloy exhibits larger He bubbles, higher irradiation hardening, and possible microstructural heterogeneity under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observed under high-temperature, helium ion irradiation conditions typical of plasma-facing components, provided that additive manufacturing processing enables the required compositional uniformity. The performance may differ if alternative processing routes or significantly different irradiation conditions are used.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports composition tailoring as beneficial for irradiation tolerance, the optimal titanium increase and the precise magnitude of improvement remain to be quantified. Long-term stability and potential trade-offs in other properties require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of refractory HEA specimens using additive manufacturing: one group with the standard (CrFeTiTa)70W30 composition and a second group with a modified composition that has an increased titanium fraction replacing part of the chromium. Subject both groups to identical helium ion irradiation at ~1023 K and reactor-relevant fluences. Post-irradiation, analyze the microstructures and mechanical properties.
measurements: Helium bubble size and density via transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Irradiation-induced hardening using nanoindentation or comparable mechanical testing
Chemical and phase homogeneity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the titanium-enriched alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in helium bubble size/density and irradiation-induced hardening compared to the baseline, or if its high-temperature mechanical strength is degraded relative to the unmodified alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the process of pursuing high-performance materials, the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [] were introduced. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

Additive Manufacturing (AM) is a rapid fabrication method that allows for unique component design, even in complex alloys such as RHEAs [,] One example of AM is laser beam directed energy deposition (LB-DED), enabling a rapid top–down near-net-shape fabrication of functionally tailored specimens [,]. AM techniques have even been proposed for fabricating compositionally and geometrically complex materials for use as plasma-facing materials in fusion reactors. However, the AM of refractory metals remains a challenge to create dense, uncracked parts without unmelted particles due to the high melting temperature, the mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients with build plates, and the intrinsic brittleness of the alloy that can be driven by high ductile-to-brittle transition temperatures. In order to overcome the issues with the AM of pure W, we pursue alloying to create dense microstructures with compositional complexity. In this work, we explore the effect of refractory alloy composition on the helium bubble characteristics produced via AM. Two-to-four component refractory alloys are compared to pure W. While pure W may have the most ideal combination of the He bubble size and density of the materials studied here, there are significant concerns for the usage of W in a fission or fusion reactor, including its ductile–brittle transition temperature, recrystallization, and the ability to fabricate complex components. The performance of additively manufactured RHEAs in other areas relevant for reactors, including fracture properties and recrystallization performance, must be explored further. Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Helium irradiation and He bubble formation and accumulation is just one aspect of materials design that should motivate materials choices for future reactors. In this work, we show that compositionally complex (spanning two, three, and four-component alloys) can be developed with AM processing routes.
